summary: Meta Horizon Worlds is a closed social platform that Meta both builds and runs: worlds are authored in Meta's own desktop editor or inside the headset, and a published world is never a file a creator can hold, because it lives in Meta's store and reaches players only through Meta's own app. The one format that crosses the wall is FBX. Custom models go in as FBX with PNG textures, and unusually for a closed platform the editor can write a whole world back out as FBX for Maya or Blender, so the geometry is not a one-way trip; but only geometry, materials and textures come back, while gizmos, scripts, lighting, colliders and everything that makes it a world stay behind. Horizon carries a great deal of meaning in names rather than in file data: collision shapes are declared by mesh-name prefixes borrowed from Unreal Engine, the material type is declared by a suffix on the material name, and the channel packing of a texture is declared by a suffix on the texture filename, and no reader outside Horizon will honour any of that. Two traps for a standards reader. Lighting is baked into vertex colours, so a model's topology must be authored for Horizon's own light and the mesh then carries that light with it, which is the opposite of how the neutral transfer formats keep the two apart. And Horizon does one thing most closed platforms refuse: a player's saved data can follow them from world to world, because a creator's variable group can be added to many worlds and shared with other creators, though only inside Horizon and only where the creators agree.

coverage.note: Horizon draws the scene itself and gives creators no way into the pipeline: there are no custom shaders, no render passes to add or reorder, and no named graphics settings. Meta's physics overview says the world uses Unity physics for core simulation on every client, and the collider page names Unity's collider components and the scripting API has a Unity asset bundle module, but physics identification alone does not establish the rendering backend or graphics interface, and Meta names neither.

coverage.note: Horizon bakes light into the vertex colours of the mesh itself, so how good the lighting looks depends on where the modeller put the vertices, and Meta tells creators to plan their topology around light and shadow before they ever import. Global illumination is precomputed in the cloud and cached with the world. Static and dynamic light gizmos exist, but a model that already carries its own lighting cannot be used in a custom model world. Every other system in this map keeps lighting and geometry apart; Horizon fuses them, so a mesh authored for Horizon arrives elsewhere with Horizon's light stuck to it.

coverage.note: This is the row that decides everything else. Horizon reads exactly one model format, FBX, with PNG textures beside it, and it reads no glTF and no USD even though Meta's own Spatial toolkit for other products reads glTF. Going the other way the desktop editor really can write an FBX of a whole world or a selection, into a folder next to the app, and Meta has since improved that export to carry several materials per object, material textures, several texture coordinate channels and mesh names. But the published world is not a container at all: it lives in Meta's store, is edited live, and only geometry, materials and textures come back out. Gizmos, scripts, colliders, lighting and saved state stay behind.

coverage.note: Material exchange happens through spelling, not through data. Meta names glTF 2.0 once, only to say its cutout threshold of one half matches. Coming the other way the export writes ordinary FBX materials and textures, which carries none of that meaning back, so material intent only ever travels inwards.

coverage.note: Horizon does not aim at the same result on two machines; it names one machine the owner and copies its answer to the rest. coverage.note: This is the best documented part of Horizon. Ownership decides which machine holds the truth for an entity and therefore where its script runs. The server owns everything by default, which keeps the view common and stops a client cheating. Ownership moves to a player automatically when they grab a thing or collide with it, or by hand from a script, and a keep-ownership-on-collision setting turns the automatic case off. Meta explains when not to hand ownership over, with worked examples of bowling pins and racing cars.

coverage.note: A review step does stand near publishing, in two parts.
